tagline.text: A protected bay in northern Palawan, home to Irrawaddy dolphins

location.label: Location
location.text: Northwest Taytay, Palawan, around Pancol pier

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,000~3,000 (boat charter for the whole boat, transport extra)

children.text: A protected bay cutting deep into northwest Taytay, and the only known habitat of the Irrawaddy dolphin in the Philippines. Hire a boat at dawn for a quiet, nature-focused trip around the bay and its mangroves.
Malampaya Sound is a bay in the municipality of Taytay on the northwest coast of Palawan. It runs about
34 km
to the southeast and is roughly
wide. Taytay lies on the northern Palawan road between El Nido and Roxas, and Malampaya Sound is the stretch of sea to its west. According to Wikipedia, it is about
217 km
north of the provincial capital, Puerto Princesa.

The area was declared the Malampaya Sound Protected Landscape and Seascape in 2000, and its land and water together are recorded at about 200,115 hectares. The inner part of the bay is a shallow brackish zone where fresh water mixes with the sea, while the outer part is deep salt water. Thirteen small islands divide the two zones, and the largest is Passage Island.

The main reason travelers come is the Irrawaddy dolphin. The inner sound of Malampaya is the only place in the Philippines known to hold this species. Numbers are so small that the IUCN lists the subpopulation as critically endangered. Dolphin watching here is therefore not a flashy show but a quiet trip in which, with luck, you watch the dolphins surface to breathe from a distance.

Around the bay you will find mangrove forests, seagrass beds, and fishing villages. Eighteen barangays of Taytay surround the bay, and the poblacion (town center) and Pancol are the largest. This is not a place with well-developed tourism infrastructure; you hire a local fisherman's boat, so the mood is completely different from an El Nido island-hopping tour. The practical options are a day trip from El Nido or a night in Taytay followed by a dawn start.
At dawn or dusk you take a boat into the inner bay and look for dolphins coming up to breathe. One blog account describes watching a pod of about six for roughly
45 minutes
. Sightings are not guaranteed, so go prepared to see nothing.

blocks.title: The only known habitat in the Philippines

children.text: This bay is the only place in the entire Philippines where Irrawaddy dolphins are known to live. A 2001 survey estimated about 77 animals, and a 2011–2012 survey estimated about 35. A U.S. NOAA document mentions an unpublished study that estimated 47 animals in 2023–2025, but it is not a published figure, so treat it as a reference only.
Mt. Capoas, which rises above the bay, is described in a trip report as an extinct volcano about
high. One travel guide site calls it the only mountain in northern Palawan with a peak of around 1,000 m. While you wait for the dolphins, the mountain slopes and calm water form a single scene.

Dolphin-watching tours are sometimes described as starting with a river cruise and gradually moving out to sea. The Abongan River and others flow into the shallow inner bay, creating a brackish environment, and mangroves and seagrass meadows line the edges. Stilt houses and fishing nets in the dawn mist make good photographs.

Many villages around the bay live from fishing and farming, and there are also Tagbanua settlements. Stilt houses, fish traps, and small boats with gill nets are everyday sights. You quickly understand why the area is described as one of Palawan's richest fishing grounds.

Irrawaddy dolphins are known in the inner bay, bottlenose dolphins in the outer sound, and Risso's dolphins at Minapla Bay. More than 156 fish species are recorded, along with dugongs, green and hawksbill sea turtles, crabs, and stingrays. The forests hold endemic species such as the Palawan binturong, Palawan pangolin, and Palawan hornbill.

blocks.title: A quiet Palawan away from El Nido

children.text: Taytay is a good base for anyone who wants to see a quieter northern Palawan away from the El Nido crowds. The 17th-century Fort Santa Isabel stands in town, so you can combine it with a dolphin tour to fill a day.
Leave your guesthouse in Taytay town and head for Pancol pier. A blog account says it was about
16 km
northwest of town and took about
30 minutes
by motorbike.

At the pier, find a boat and boatman. There is often no fixed booking desk, so it is safer to ask local fishermen directly or arrange contact in advance through your guesthouse or a travel agency. Confirm the price, the duration, and whether fuel is included before you set out.
Head into the inner bay and look for dolphins. Turn the engine off early and wait quietly, and you may see the dolphins surface to breathe. Do not chase them; keep your distance.
After a tour of about
2 hours
, return to the pier. One guide site also describes a version of the tour that includes breakfast on the shore afterward.
Return to Taytay town to see Fort Santa Isabel, or continue toward El Nido or Roxas.
Dolphins are said to be most active around dawn and dusk, but there is no fixed time. It depends on the weather and tides.
Leave El Nido by private vehicle or motorbike. Taytay is about
60 km
by road. Early-morning travel is dark and the road can be rough, so talk it over with a local driver.
Find a boat at Pancol pier and spend about
2 hours
watching for dolphins.
Have lunch in Taytay, see the fort, and return to El Nido.
It can be done in one day, but the road conditions and the early start are demanding. If you have time, an overnight stay in Taytay is recommended.
The most common way is a flight from Manila to Puerto Princesa International Airport (PPS). Check the latest schedules for flights and times.
From Puerto Princesa, Taytay is about
217 km
to the north. You travel by bus or van, and the time varies greatly with road conditions and stops.
You can also fly directly to El Nido and continue to Taytay overland. Whether those flights operate changes by season, so check the latest announcements.

items.title: Overland from El Nido or Puerto Princesa

children.text: Pancol is on the national highway linking Puerto Princesa and El Nido. Trip reports describe taking a bus or van, getting off at the Pancol junction, and walking a short distance to the pier.
From El Nido to Taytay town it is about
60 km
by road. The travel time depends on stops and road surface.
Bus and van timetables and fares change often and seats are limited, so ask at your accommodation first.

items.title: From Taytay town to the pier

children.text: A blog account says Pancol is about
16 km
from town, roughly
30 minutes
by motorbike. Taytay has no motorbike rental shops, and one visitor borrowed a bike from a local, so it is usually better to rent in Puerto Princesa or El Nido and bring it.
You can also negotiate for a tricycle or a private vehicle. Arrange early-morning transport the day before.
The starting point of dolphin tours varies by account, from Pancol pier to the edge of town. Be sure to confirm the departure point when you book.

For dolphin watching, the time of day matters more than anything. Trip reports recommend early morning or late afternoon, and one guide site says dolphin pods hunt for food at sunrise. One blogger left town at 6 a.m., found a boat around 7 a.m., and met a pod around 8 a.m.

As for season, the dry months with lower waves and steadier weather are better. Sightings, however, depend more on the day's sea conditions and the dolphins' movements than on the season, so it is wise to allow one or two spare days. In the rainy and typhoon seasons, check locally whether boats are running.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Many calm days, well suited to dawn tours
Midday sun is strong, so use the dawn hours
Rainy season, frequent rain and wind
Tours may be canceled depending on waves and weather, so leave some slack in your schedule

Staying in Taytay town (the poblacion) is the most convenient for a dawn tour. Older travel guides list simple lodgings such as Casa Rosa Inn, Perm's Pension House, and Tay Lelong's Pension. Rates and whether they still operate may have changed, so confirm before booking. Do not expect large resorts.

The town has a small market and restaurants. Casa Rosa's restaurant was known for its pizza and its view over the fort and the bay. Before an early departure, check that breakfast is available, and bring snacks and drinking water. An older guide also records that electricity was supplied only at night, so ask your lodging in advance about charging and cooling.

Before choosing a tour, ask whether it is currently authorized, where it starts, how many boats may approach the animals at once, and what happens if the weather or the dolphins' absence cancels the trip.
Move at dawn. According to one account, leaving town around 6 a.m. still allowed finding a boat around 7 a.m.
Turning the engine off early and waiting quietly makes it more likely the dolphins will surface without being startled.
Keep at least
from the dolphins. Do not approach unless they come to the boat on their own.
Binoculars or a telephoto lens help a lot. Dolphins surface briefly and disappear again.
Bring plenty of cash. Cards are often not accepted at rural piers.
Bring sun protection, a hat, and a waterproof bag, and take all your trash back with you.
Dolphins are protected wildlife, so never chase or herd them. Sightings are not guaranteed, and if the dolphins seem disturbed, leave right away.
Do not swim with, touch, or feed the dolphins. Also avoid surrounding a group or changing direction suddenly.
When renting a local fisherman's boat that has no formal booking system, check for safety equipment and life jackets. One account reports a late start because of a fuel shortage.
If many boats crowd in at once, the dolphins flee. Avoid spots that are too busy.
The El Nido–Taytay road can be in poor condition, and an older record notes heavy dust in the dry season. Be careful on early-morning motorbike rides.
Tour prices, permit status, and protected-area rules can change, so check the latest local announcements just before you go.
A 17th-century fort on the Taytay waterfront, easy to visit on foot before or after a dolphin tour.
About
60 km
from Taytay by road, northern Palawan's tourism hub, with island tours and beaches.
A long beach south of Taytay, toward Puerto Princesa.
The provincial capital of Palawan, about
217 km
south of Malampaya Sound. It is the main gateway for flights.
